newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees no quick answer to NATO row with France.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees no quick answer to NATO row with France.

text.p: A dispute between the United States and France over who should command NATO's southern flank was unlikely to be settled at a meeting of NATO foreign ministers next week, the State Department said on Wednesday.

The Naples-based position has always been held by an American but France is now pressing for the key post, which controls allied forces in the Mediterranean, to be given to a European. So far, Washington has refused.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, calling it a "very serious disagreement", said: "I don't expect that it will be resolved by next week because of the serious differences that exist."
Foreign ministers of the 16-nation alliance hold their regular winter meeting in Brussels next Tuesday.
"It'll get resolved at some point in the future," Burns told a news briefing in response to a question.

"The United States position is the Sixth Fleet is the basis of the command... the Sixth Fleet is an American fleet, it ought to be commanded by an American, it's always been commanded by an American," Burns said.
"I don't think the Congress or the American people would understand it if our troops and our naval forces, the largest armada in the world, were to be commanded by anyone but an American."
But Burns said Washington hoped the "courageous efforts" of French President Jacques Chirac to bring France back into NATO's military structure, from which it withdrew in 1966, would be continued.
"NATO is stronger because of French involvement and we'll continue to work cooperatively with the French and respectfully disagree on this particular issue," he said.
